content_voiceover: Primary cutaneous ALCL is a distinct entity from systemic ALCL, and the immunophenotype is your first clue: it's ALK negative and EMA negative, but strongly CD30 positive, placing it within the spectrum of CD30 positive cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorders alongside lymphomatoid papulosis. It typically occurs in older patients and, importantly, carries a much better prognosis than systemic ALCL, with about twenty-five percent of lesions undergoing spontaneous regression without any treatment at all. First line treatment is local excision, with or without radiotherapy, reflecting the generally indolent, localized behavior of this disease. A key differential diagnosis to keep in mind is lymphomatoid papulosis, since the two conditions can look strikingly similar clinically and histologically, and distinguishing them relies on the overall clinical course, lesion size, and behavior over time rather than any single marker.
keypoints: ALK negative, EMA negative, CD30 positive cutaneous lymphoma
Part of the CD30+ cutaneous lymphoproliferative disorder spectrum
Better prognosis than systemic ALCL; 25% show spontaneous regression
Treatment: excision with or without radiotherapy
keypoint_voiceover: Remember primary cutaneous ALCL as the good actor of the CD30 positive skin lymphomas: ALK negative, older patients, a quarter regress on their own, and excision with or without radiation is usually sufficient. Don't confuse it with lymphomatoid papulosis, its close mimic on the same disease spectrum.
